## Logger class

The `Logger` class implements the logger functionality.

**Signature:**

```typescript
export declare class Logger<C extends LoggerConsole = Console> 
```

## Remarks

The package is an ES module; CommonJS code can load it with `require()` on Node.js 22.12 or later.

The description has sections on the empty messages, the logging methods, extending the class, the timestamps, the prefix and the expansion of an `Error`<!-- -->, the untrusted input, and the preliminary state and its cost.

The logger is constructed on top of a console object, where the messages are logged. The class has a type parameter, the type of the console, so that the `console` accessor returns the object that was passed, with its own type: a `Logger` without a console is a `Logger<Console>`<!-- -->, and a logger constructed with a `MockConsole` is a `Logger<MockConsole>`<!-- -->, whose `console` accessor gives access to the members of the mock without a cast. The type must have the `log()` and `error()` functions (see `LoggerConsole`<!-- -->). Since a logger without a console uses the JavaScript standard `console` object, the console can be omitted only if that object is of the type `C`<!-- -->; for a richer type, like `Logger<MockConsole>`<!-- -->, it is required, and the compiler rejects the constructor call without it.

Use `log.always()` instead of the `console.log()`<!-- -->, since it writes on the console of the logger, so a test can capture it with a mock console and a subclass can intercept it with `write()`<!-- -->; in the preliminary state it is buffered, like the other messages.

The log levels, from the lowest to the highest, are `silent`<!-- -->, `error`<!-- -->, `warn`<!-- -->, `info`<!-- -->, `verbose`<!-- -->, `debug`<!-- -->, `trace`<!-- -->, and `all`<!-- -->. A higher level writes more messages: a message is written when the log level is equal to or higher than the level of its method. The `error` and `warn` levels are for problems, `info` and `verbose` for the progress of the application, `debug` and `trace` for the details needed to diagnose it, `silent` writes only the messages of `always()`<!-- -->, and `all` writes everything.

There is no `critical` level, corresponding to errors that prevent the program from running, since these are actually related to bugs; use `assert()` from `node:assert` instead.

The messages may include formatting directives, with additional arguments, as defined by the Node.js `Console` (template literals are often simpler).

All logging methods accept an optional message, of any type, and possibly some arguments, as processed by the standard Node.js [util.format()](https://nodejs.org/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args) function.

<b>Empty messages.</b> If the message is omitted or `undefined`<!-- -->, it is replaced by an empty string, so `log.info()` writes an empty line, and the methods with a prefix write only the prefix; this differs from `console.log()`<!-- -->, which writes `undefined`<!-- -->. The other values, and the details, are in the section "Empty messages" of the User's Guide.

<b>Logging methods.</b> The methods differ by the level from which they are written (the threshold), by the console stream, and by a prefix added to the message:

<table> <thead> <tr><th>Method</th><th>Written from level</th> <th>Stream</th><th>Prefix</th></tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr><td><code>always()</code></td><td>every level</td> <td>stdout</td><td>none</td></tr> <tr><td><code>error()</code></td><td><code>error</code></td> <td>stderr</td><td><code>error: </code></td></tr> <tr><td><code>output()</code></td><td><code>error</code></td> <td>stdout</td><td>none</td></tr> <tr><td><code>warn()</code></td><td><code>warn</code></td> <td>stderr</td><td><code>warning: </code></td></tr> <tr><td><code>info()</code></td><td><code>info</code></td> <td>stdout</td><td>none</td></tr> <tr><td><code>verbose()</code></td><td><code>verbose</code></td> <td>stdout</td><td>none</td></tr> <tr><td><code>debug()</code></td><td><code>debug</code></td> <td>stdout</td><td><code>debug: </code></td></tr> <tr><td><code>trace()</code></td><td><code>trace</code></td> <td>stdout</td><td><code>trace: </code></td></tr> </tbody> </table>

Here stdout is `console.log()` and stderr is `console.error()`<!-- -->. A method is written when the log level is equal to or higher than its threshold; at `silent` only `always()` is written. The method `error()` omits its prefix when the first argument is an `Error` (see below).

The three methods that write on stdout without a prefix are used for different purposes:

<ul> <li><code>always()</code> is for the messages that must be shown at every log level, including <code>silent</code>, like the version or the result requested by the user;</li> <li><code>output()</code> is for the normal output of the application, which is suppressed at <code>silent</code>, together with all the other messages;</li> <li><code>info()</code> is for informative messages, shown from the <code>info</code> level.</li> </ul>

<b>Extending the class.</b> A subclass can intercept the messages by overriding the protected `write()` method, which is the only supported extension point (see its description for the contract). The state of the logger is private; use the public members, like `level`<!-- -->, `hasLevel`<!-- -->, `isLevel()`<!-- -->, and `console`<!-- -->. The protected members that gave direct access to the state (`_console`<!-- -->, `levelNumericValue`<!-- -->, `levelName`<!-- -->, and `buffer`<!-- -->) are deprecated, still work, and will be removed in the next major version.

<b>Timestamps.</b> If the logger is created with the `timestamp` option, the messages of the methods that have a prefix start with the local time, and the prefix is replaced by the kind of the message in square brackets; the format and the rules are in the description of the `timestamp` accessor.

<b>Errors.</b> An `Error` passed to a logging method is expanded with its stack trace and its `cause` chain, and `error()` omits its prefix for it; the details, and how to show only the message, are in the description of `error()`<!-- -->.

<b>Untrusted input.</b> The messages are written as they are, without any escaping, so text that comes from outside the application can forge messages, send control sequences to the terminal, and be interpreted as format directives. Pass such text as an argument, never as the first argument, with a constant format string, for example `log.info('user: %j', name)`<!-- -->, where `%j` also escapes the newlines and the control characters; see the section "Logging untrusted input" of the User's Guide.

To skip the preparation of a message when the message would not be written, check the level first, with `isDebugEnabled` or the other checks of the level; see the section "Log level checks" of the User's Guide.

There are cases when the logger must be created very early in the life cycle of an application, even before it is practically possible to determine the log level.

For these cases, if the logger is created without a log level, it is in a <b>preliminary state</b>, and all messages are stored in an <b>internal buffer</b>, until the log level is set, when the buffer is replayed and the messages are written.

Nothing is written while the logger is in the preliminary state, not even the messages of `always()` and `error()`<!-- -->. If the log level is never set (for example when the application fails before it determines the level), the buffered messages are never written and are lost. Set the log level on every path, for example in a `catch` or `finally` block, using `hasLevel` to check whether it was set. The example and the cost of the preliminary state, which formats and stores every message, are in the section "Delaying setting the log level" of the User's Guide.

## Example


```javascript
import { Logger } from '@xpack/logger'

const log = new Logger({ level: 'info' })
log.info('Started') // Started
log.debug('Details') // Nothing, since `debug` is above the level.
log.error('Failed') // error: Failed, on the standard error.
```
